title: Faxiang's Created World
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of letting go of our ego and self-concept, which can lead to suffering and conditioning. By embracing humility and a sense of service, we can cultivate a more authentic and compassionate way of being. This involves recognizing that our true nature is not defined by our thoughts or actions, but rather by our ability to respond without attachment or expectation, allowing us to tap into our inner strength and wisdom.

sentences.text: Hi.
The next month, June, is our guiding teacher Tim's annual sabbatical, a month-long break.
So the dharma talks are being given by some of the other practice leaders in this group.

We thought we'd be speaking about some of the stories from this book, The Hidden Lamp, Stories from Twenty-Five Centuries of Awakened Women, edited by Zenshin Florence Caplow and Reigetsu Susan Moon, who are members of our Everyday Zen community.
So tonight maybe we can jump into June for a little bit with a story of which the two characters are Zen nuns.
This story touches on several of our common core Zen topics: the emptiness or the boundlessness of self, what is true generosity, and meditation.
*The nun Franny often shared her clothing and food, giving the best to another nun, Heather.
The other nuns admonished Franny, saying, "Heather is uncultivated and inarticulate.
When she was learning to meditate, no one could stand to teach her because she is the worst of idiots.
Why don't you sow the seeds of generosity in a more spiritually worthy field?"
Franny responded, "When giving a donation, you'd have to be a saint to know the spiritual accomplishments of the recipient.
I'm a very ordinary person, so I would rather do it this way."
One day, Heather organized a seven day meditation retreat with the community.
On the third night when the others arose from meditation, she did not get up, remaining in a deep meditation state until the end of the retreat.
It was only then that the other nuns saw Heather's extraordinary abilities, and for the first time they understood Franny's insight.*
A part of that story that stuck with me is this notion of ordinary person, and looking at the great lengths we go to to protect the self.
Most of our problems, most of our arguments, our anger and frustration and sadness can be traced back to an effort to defend this concept of self.
Actually, I changed the names in that story to make them a little more familiar.
The story is from the fifth century of the common era.
Franny's actual name is Fao Zhang and Heather's name is Huisu.
Still, we're stuck on this notion of self that we defend.

When I say that, we usually think about defending the greatness of the self, but we also often make it a point of defending ourselves, defending aspects we consider to be ourselves which are contrary to our values, bending our perception of the world to maintain the concept of ourselves as being someone who is a mean person or a helpless person.

There's a lot of Zen discussion about the importance of the emptiness, the boundlessness of the self, and there's a danger in all that discussion of passing over this person in our love of all beings.
There's a conversation going on in the medical community around the world right now with the word "just."
It was started by a Facebook post from an Australian nurse.
She wrote, over my 18-year career, I've heard this phrase many, many times, but today it got to me.
No, I'm missing a piece.
A friend saw her at the store in her scrubs and said, "Oh, I didn't realize you were just a nurse."
Am I just a nurse?
I have helped babies into the world, many of whom needed assistance to take their first breath, and yet I am just a nurse, she wrote.
I have held patients' hands and ensured their dignity while they take their last breath, and yet I am just a nurse.
I have counseled grieving patients after the loss of a child, and yet I am just a nurse.
I am the medical officer's eyes, ears, and hands, with the ability to assess, treat, and manage your illness, and yet I am just a nurse.
If I am just a nurse, then I am ridiculously proud to be one.
That, hey, wait a minute, let's take a second look every time we're about to use that word, "just," has been important to me for years.

That above story: there was a Cleveland doctor then at Beachwood Family Health Clinic. [unclear: "Cleveland was thinking"] about this post as he was getting to know a medical assistant, filling in for a sick medical assistant in his ear, nose, and throat office, when she said, "I am just a float," or a substitute.
And he was like, in this scenario, on a busy day in the office when we're one medical assistant short, no one was more important to us than a float medical assistant.
So we asked her to repeat her answer with pride, without the word "just": "I am a float and my name is..."
He recounted the experience in an email to his staff, writing, I hope she enjoyed what she did and that she did it with pride and with an appropriate sense of being a key part of our team that day.
I have heard myself say, I am just a general otolaryngologist.
I have heard others say, I am just a receptionist.
I have even heard someone say, I am just a medical director in a smaller family health care.
So let's lose the word "just."
We can describe ourselves without the word "just," without losing the humility that we hopefully all feel as well.
If you hear someone say it to describe themselves, gently correct them.
I'm just saying, whoops, I'm saying, let's have pride in what we do as individuals and as a team.
So how do we find some middle ground between the harmful diminutive view of self and a harmful creation of self?
Then coming back to that story of the ordinary person and the idiot, what we see to be an idiot.
We chant the Jewel Mirror Samadhi, saying we're going to practice secretly, working within like a fool, like an idiot.
When we chant Dogen's Fukanzazengi, he says, *intelligence or lack of it does not matter.

Between the dull and the sharp-witted, there is no distinction.* And later on, *we should therefore cease from practice based on intellectual understanding, pursuing words and following after speech, and learn the backward step that turns your light inwardly to illuminate yourself.*
A bunch of concepts tie together here.
There's this notion of an inward truer self that's not the one that we are shaping the world to make ourselves look like.
There's the notion that intelligence doesn't get us to the point of compassion or realizing what the study of this practice we're doing here tonight is.
That's not to say we shouldn't be studying.
We've got a whole library of books there, and we hope that we all have opportunities to check them out and to study.
But then we need to go beyond that.
Clarity is not about abandoning thinking completely.
As Scott quoted the Blue Cliff Record during his Shuso ceremony, saying, *the way has nothing to do with knowing or not knowing.
Knowing is an exaggeration and not knowing is stupidity.* So we need some thinking, and thinking gets in the way.
Looking at Fo Zhang's story, aka Franny, [unclear: "Taoiseach Shunjian Merrill"] wrote in The Hidden Lamp that Fo Zhang's story is everyone's story.
How do we sincerely practice the paramita, the perfection of generosity, without falling into dualistic thinking?
Our usual understanding of generosity is that there is one who gives materials, things, time, energy, and one who receives them.
In the creation of giver and receiver, however, we are already lost in delusion, misunderstanding the fundamental nature of generosity, ending separation between self and other.
The fundamental nature of generosity is ending the separation between self and other.
Because this self is just something that we are putting together.
There was a day when I was complaining, after a bunch of things had gone wrong, about why is everybody doing this shit to me?
A wise friend of mine said, they're not.
They're just doing their shit.
It's my twisting of the world to turn all of that back onto me.

Just as Dogen is considered the founder of the Soto school of Zen in Japan, our lineage, Linji, pronounced Rinzai in Japanese, is considered to be the origin of the other primary surviving school, the Rinzai school.
One characteristic term used by Linji was "the true person of no rank," which kind of brings us back to that ordinary person.
The true person of no rank.
Koan number 38 in the Book of Serenity is the most well known story involving Linji's use of that phrase.
*One day Master Linji said, "There is a true person of no rank, always going in and out from your facial features.
Those who have not yet testified, look, look."* The true person is the inner self we were talking about earlier, the one that's called the original self or the unconditioned, the Buddha nature.
Just this bit about rank.
The true person of no rank.
When we rank things, we choose our preferences for one thing over another, and those preferences are our conditioned responses to the world.
When we go beyond this false self that we've created to the true self, there are not those created preferences.
Incidentally, that koan continues.
*A monk came forward and said, "Who is the true person of no rank?"
Master Rinzai came down from his seat,* you can tell I changed translation there from Rinzai to Linji, *came down from his seat, grabbed the monk and held him.
The monk hesitated,* which in the Zen teaching means there's some blockage there.
*Master Rinzai let go and said, "What a dried up shit stick the true man of no rank is."* Meaning, yeah, he didn't quite have it.
He wasn't able to respond.
And the thing to know is that it's okay to be a dried up shit stick.

In his talk on this koan, Norman Fischer says, *those of you who know me know that I'm always trying to explain things and give talks that are clear and that make sense, because I think it's worthwhile and important to understand what we're doing in practice and why we're doing it.
But I really am quite aware of the limitations of doing this.
It really only goes so far.
And if I create the misperception that just listen to what I say and you'll get the idea, that's not really what I mean.
What I'm saying only goes so far.
In the end, the practice, the actual practice, is something far more immediate than this.
It's not what we explain, it's what we live.* And Master Linji was really good about not giving any explanations at all, not creating any misperceptions about what we were doing.
Instead, forcing people with his short style to live rather than to think about the teaching.
Again, we've got the teaching.
We still pay attention to the teaching, but then we let it go and we live.
And maybe clear up some of that confusion that we're making up.
These bibs that some of the students are wearing are a representation of Buddha's robe.
At the sewing retreat that Chris held a few weeks ago, we were chanting the merit of the Kasaya, the merit of Buddha's robe, from Dogen's Shobogenzo, although he was quoting a much older sutra.
There's language in there about how this protects you from heat, cold, and poisonous creatures.
*And a dragon who wears even a shred of the Kasaya cannot be devoured by a gold-winged Garuda,* which is an eagle-headed giant.
Where does that come from?
There are a lot of stories in the older text about what couldn't possibly be true.

Supernatural powers of Buddhas and advanced practitioners include changing form, passing through objects, turning invisible, mind reading, teleportation, illumination, and the conjuring of creatures and images.
But all of that stuff is no less true than the stories that we're making up continuously every day.
No less true than my story that everybody's doing what they're doing just to get me.

My experience is that the more clearly I'm able to be in touch with the error in this notion of self, the more I can touch the creation of that story involving all these characters and all these characters and this character.
Eventually the magic and miracles that are described in stories everywhere no longer seem far-fetched.
Another story from The Hidden Lamp, this one from the 12th century.
The laywoman Yu Daopo made donuts for a living, and she also studied Chan, or Zen, with Master Linji.
Actually, no, she studied with Lange, but he assigned her Linji's phrase that we talked about earlier, the true person of no rank.
One day she and her husband were delivering donuts, and as they walked through the street they [unclear: "made a beggar"] who was singing, "Happiness in the Lotus Land."
Yu was suddenly enlightened and threw the tray of donuts to the ground.
Her husband scolded her, "Have you gone crazy?" [unclear: "You slapped him"], saying, "This is not a realm you understand."
Not meaning that he was failing to understand, meaning this realm, this realm of happiness, is not about understanding.
She then went to see Lange, who immediately verified her awakening.
One day after this, Lange said to the assembly, "Which one is the true person of no rank?"
And Yu stood up and shouted out this verse:
*There is a true person of no rank, who has six arms and three heads.
When she uses her full strength to cut, Mount Hua is split in two.
Her strength is like the ever flowing water, not caring about the coming of spring.*
You are Yu Dao Po, and I am you Dao Po.
You have the strength of ever flowing water that can split the mountains that block your way.
That strength is just there, and it just takes the relinquishing of the distinction between giver, receiver and gift.
So what story are you and me going to tell tomorrow?
Will we manage to see beyond the idiots, especially this one?
Will we manage to see beyond uncultivated and inarticulate?
Huh, we'll find out.
May God bless you.
